name: Advanced YARA Rule Development — pe/math Modules, yarGen & Real-World Rules
description: Advanced YARA techniques for APT/malware detection. YARA modules extend rules: import "pe" gives pe.imphash(), pe.number_of_sections, pe.number_of_resources, pe.resources[i]; import "math" gives math.entropy() for packed/encrypted sections. .NET assembly detection: BSJB magic bytes (42 53 4A 42) at CLI header = .NET artifact. yarGen workflow: update goodware DB first, then generate from samples dir, then tune. Real-world rules: APT17 ZoxPNG by imphash, Neuron Service by .NET BSJB string, Stonedrill Shamoon2 by high entropy + resource ID 101.
source: CDSA Module 12: YARA & Sigma for SOC Analysts
notes:
=== YARA MODULES OVERVIEW ===
Modules extend YARA with structured access to file internals.
Import at top of rule file:
  import "pe"
  import "math"

=== pe MODULE ===

pe.imphash()
  → Import hash — hash of all imported function names in order
  → SAME malware family often shares imphash even across recompiles
  → If two samples have identical imphash → likely same codebase

  Example (APT17 ZoxPNG rule):
    import "pe"
    rule APT17_ZoxPNG {
        meta:
            description = "Detects APT17 ZoxPNG RAT via import hash"
            author = "Florian Roth"
        condition:
            pe.imphash() == "414bbd566b700ea021cfae3ad8f4d9b9"
    }

pe.number_of_sections
  → Count of PE sections (e.g., .text, .data, .rsrc)
  → Unusual section counts can indicate packing or malware
  → Most legitimate PE files: 3-8 sections

pe.number_of_resources
  → Count of resources (icons, strings, version info, etc.)
  → Malware embedding shellcode in resources → often 1-2 resources

pe.resources[i].id
  → Resource ID at index i
  → Stonedrill embeds dropper as resource with specific ID
  → Access: pe.resources[0].id == 101

pe.resources[i].offset
  → Byte offset of resource data in file

pe.resources[i].length
  → Size of resource in bytes

=== math MODULE ===

math.entropy(offset, size)
  → Shannon entropy of a byte range in the file
  → Range: 0 (all same byte) to 8 (maximum randomness)
  → Threshold: > 7.0 = highly packed/encrypted (suspicious)
  → Normal binaries: ~6.0-7.0 for code sections

Detecting encrypted/packed overlay:
  math.entropy(0, filesize) > 7.0

Detecting high-entropy resource:
  math.entropy(pe.resources[0].offset, pe.resources[0].length) > 7.0

Stonedrill/Shamoon2 example:
  import "pe"
  import "math"
  rule Stonedrill_Wiper {
      meta:
          description = "Detects Stonedrill wiper via high-entropy resource"
      condition:
          pe.number_of_resources == 1 and
          pe.resources[0].id == 101 and
          math.entropy(pe.resources[0].offset, pe.resources[0].length) > 7.0
  }

=== .NET ASSEMBLY DETECTION ===
All .NET executables contain a CLI header with 'BSJB' magic bytes:
  → ASCII string: 'BSJB'
  → Hex: 42 53 4A 42
  → Located in the CLI (Common Language Infrastructure) header
  → Present in ALL .NET assemblies (executables and DLLs)

Detect .NET binary in YARA:
  rule Is_DotNET {
      strings:
          $bsjb = "BSJB"
      condition:
          uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and
          $bsjb
  }

monodis tool (Linux) — disassemble .NET assemblies:
  monodis /path/to/assembly.exe
  → Outputs: class names, method names, IL instructions
  → Use to identify unique strings/classes for YARA detection
  → Look for: class names, namespace names, string literals in IL

Finding unique strings from .NET with strings:
  strings -a assembly.exe | grep -i 'UniqueClassName'

Neuron Service (Turla APT) example:
  rule Neuron_Service {
      meta:
          description = "Detects Neuron malware .NET service"
      strings:
          $s1 = "NeuronService" fullword ascii
          $s2 = "Execute" fullword ascii
      condition:
          uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and
          $s1 and $s2 and
          $bsjb  // $bsjb defined separately or as:
          // (for inline: uint32(pe.directories[14].virtual_address) == 0x424A5342)
  }

=== UPX PACKER DETECTION ===
UPX-packed binaries have distinctive section names:
  → Sections named: UPX0, UPX1, UPX2
  → PE header section names are at fixed offsets

Simple UPX detection string rule:
  rule UPX_Packed {
      strings:
          $upx0 = "UPX0"
          $upx1 = "UPX1"
      condition:
          uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and
          all of them
  }

=== yarGen DETAILED WORKFLOW ===
yarGen = YARA Rule Generator by Florian Roth
  → Extracts unique strings from malware
  → Compares against goodware DB to exclude common strings
  → Output: ready-to-use YARA rules

Step 1: Update goodware database (first time ONLY):
  cd /home/htb-student/yarGen
  python3 yarGen.py --update
  → Downloads ~100MB of known-good string databases
  → Must run before first use or strings won't be filtered

Step 2: Generate rule from a sample directory:
  python3 yarGen.py -m /home/htb-student/Samples/ -o /home/htb-student/rules.yar
  → -m: path to malware sample(s) — file or directory
  → -o: output .yar file path
  → Creates one rule per sample file
  → Rule names auto-generated from filename

Step 3: Review and tune generated rules:
  → Remove overly generic strings (short, common substrings)
  → Verify condition makes sense (default: 1 of ($s*))
  → Add metadata: author, date, reference, description
  → Test against clean samples: run on known-good directory → expect 0 matches
  → Tune score threshold if yarGen has a scoring mode

Example generated rule output:
  rule dharma_sample {
      meta:
          description = "Auto-generated rule - file dharma_sample.exe"
          author = "yarGen Rule Generator"
      strings:
          $s1 = "Carbanak" fullword ascii
          $s2 = "ransom_dharma" fullword wide
          ...
      condition:
          uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and ( 1 of ($s*) )
  }

=== APT17 / ZoxPNG — IMPHASH-BASED RULE ===
Real-world case: APT17 used ZoxPNG RAT tool
  → All samples shared same import table → same imphash
  → Most reliable indicator across variants

Manual imphash check:
  pefile Python library:
    python3 -c "import pefile; pe=pefile.PE('sample.exe'); print(pe.get_imphash())"

Imphash-based rule:
  import "pe"
  rule APT17_ZoxPNG {
      meta:
          description = "Detects APT17 ZoxPNG RAT via import hash"
          hash1 = "0375b4216334c85a4b29441a3d37e61d"
          author = "Florian Roth"
          date = "2016-03-26"
      condition:
          pe.imphash() == "414bbd566b700ea021cfae3ad8f4d9b9"
  }

=== COMBINING TECHNIQUES IN ONE RULE ===
Best practice: combine multiple weak indicators = strong rule

  import "pe"
  import "math"
  rule Example_Robust_Malware_Detection {
      meta:
          description = "Detects example malware via multiple indicators"
      strings:
          $s1 = "evil_string" fullword ascii
          $s2 = "c2domain.com" fullword ascii nocase
          $pdb = "\\.pdb" ascii
          $bsjb = "BSJB"                    // if .NET
      condition:
          uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and
          filesize < 2MB and
          pe.number_of_sections > 2 and
          math.entropy(0, filesize) > 6.5 and
          2 of ($s*) and
          not $pdb                           // exclude debug builds
  }

=== ONLINE HUNTING RESOURCE ===
Unpac.Me: https://www.unpac.me/
  → Upload sample → automatic unpacking (UPX, etc.)
  → Run YARA rules against unpacked samples
  → YARA Hunt: search their DB of samples with your rule
  → Useful for testing rules against a large malware corpus
